The Kummer–Dedekind Theorem

Introduction

Let KKK be a number field of degree nnn with ring of integers OK\OO_KOK​. A rational prime ppp generates an ideal pOKp\OO_KpOK​, and unique factorization of ideals in the Dedekind domain OK\OO_KOK​ gives us pOK=q1e1⋯qgeg p\OO_K=\mfq_1^{e_1}\cdots\mfq_g^{e_g} pOK​=q1e1​​⋯qgeg​​ for distinct prime ideals q1,…,qg\mfq_1,\dots,\mfq_gq1​,…,qg​ of OK\OO_KOK​, the primes lying over ppp. The existence of this factorization is a theorem, but how do we calculate it? Given KKK and ppp, what are the primes qi\mfq_iqi​, what are the exponents eie_iei​, and what are the residue fields OK/qi\OO_K/\mfq_iOK​/qi​?

Here is the same question in a different costume. Let CCC be a plane curve f(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0 over R\RRR, and project it onto the xxx-axis. Above a point ccc of the axis sit finitely many points of CCC, some of them perhaps tangent to the vertical line x=cx=cx=c, some of them perhaps complex rather than real. Given fff and ccc, what is the fiber over ccc, with its multiplicities and its fields of definition?

The Kummer–Dedekind theorem answers both questions at once, and with the same proof. In both settings there is a base ring AAA, namely Z\ZZZ or R[x]\RR[x]R[x], a monic polynomial fff with coefficients in AAA, and the ring A[α]≅A[x]/(f)A[\alpha]\cong A[x]/(f)A[α]≅A[x]/(f) obtained by adjoining a root. The theorem says that the primes of A[α]A[\alpha]A[α] over a prime p\mfpp of AAA mirror the factorization of fff modulo p\mfpp: each irreducible factor of f mod pf\bmod\mfpfmodp gives a prime, its degree gives the residue field, and its multiplicity gives the exponent. Factoring ideals, which sounds hard, is reduced to factoring a polynomial over a residue field, which is a finite computation.

The theorem comes in three parts, and the point of this note is to be clear about which hypotheses each part uses. Part I needs nothing beyond the presentation A[α]≅A[x]/(f)A[\alpha]\cong A[x]/(f)A[α]≅A[x]/(f). Part II, which upgrades a containment of ideals to an actual factorization, needs the primes over p\mfpp to be invertible ideals, which is automatic when A[α]A[\alpha]A[α] is a Dedekind domain. Part III explains how to use the theorem when A[α]A[\alpha]A[α] is not the full ring of integers, or not the coordinate ring of a smooth curve, which is where the condition “ppp does not divide the index [OK:Z[α]][\OO_K:\ZZ[\alpha]][OK​:Z[α]]” comes from.

A word on history. Kummer worked out this description of prime factorizations in 1847 for the cyclotomic fields Q(ζp)\QQ(\zeta_p)Q(ζp​) [1], before the general notion of an ideal existed; Chapter 4 of Edwards [2] recounts his work. Dedekind proved the general statement in 1878 [3], in the same paper that introduced the obstruction we meet in Section 5; Conrad's note [4] points to the relevant pages. Modern textbook treatments are Theorem 27 of Marcus [5] and Chapter 3 of Milne [6].

1. The setting

Throughout, AAA is a Dedekind domain with fraction field KKK, and f∈A[x]f\in A[x]f∈A[x] is a monic polynomial of degree nnn that is irreducible in K[x]K[x]K[x]. Let α\alphaα be a root of fff in some extension of KKK, let L=K(α)L=K(\alpha)L=K(α), a field of degree nnn over KKK, and let B:=A[α]⊆L. B := A[\alpha]\subseteq L. B:=A[α]⊆L. The evaluation map A[x]→A[α]A[x]\to A[\alpha]A[x]→A[α], x↦αx\mapsto\alphax↦α, is surjective, and its kernel is the ideal (f)(f)(f). Therefore B≅A[x]/(f), B\cong A[x]/(f), B≅A[x]/(f), and BBB is a free AAA-module with basis 1,α,…,αn−11,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}1,α,…,αn−1. This presentation is the only structural fact about BBB that Part I of the theorem uses.

Remark (Why the kernel is exactly (f)(f)(f))

If h∈A[x]h\in A[x]h∈A[x] satisfies h(α)=0h(\alpha)=0h(α)=0, then fff divides hhh in K[x]K[x]K[x], since fff is irreducible and monic, hence the minimal polynomial of α\alphaα over KKK. Because fff is monic, long division of hhh by fff never introduces denominators, so the quotient already lies in A[x]A[x]A[x] and fff divides hhh in A[x]A[x]A[x]. Monicness is doing real work here: for a non-monic fff the ring A[α]A[\alpha]A[α] is not a quotient of A[x]A[x]A[x] by (f)(f)(f), and need not be finitely generated as an AAA-module.

There are two essential example settings we will consider.

Number fields. Take A=ZA=\ZZA=Z, so K=QK=\QQK=Q. Then fff is the minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer α\alphaα, L=Q(α)L=\QQ(\alpha)L=Q(α) is a number field, and B=Z[α]B=\ZZ[\alpha]B=Z[α]. The primes of AAA are the prime numbers ppp, with residue fields Fp\FpFp​.

Plane curves. Take A=R[x]A=\RR[x]A=R[x], so K=R(x)K=\RR(x)K=R(x), the field of rational functions in xxx. A monic polynomial in A[y]A[y]A[y] is a polynomial f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y) in two variables whose highest power of yyy has coefficient 111, such as y2−xy^2-xy2−x or y2−x2(x+1)y^2-x^2(x+1)y2−x2(x+1). Then B=R[x,y]/(f)B=\RR[x,y]/(f)B=R[x,y]/(f) is the ring of polynomial functions on the curve C ⁣:f(x,y)=0C\colon f(x,y)=0C:f(x,y)=0, and the inclusion A⊆BA\subseteq BA⊆B corresponds geometrically to the projection of CCC onto the xxx-axis. The primes of AAA that we will look at are pc=(x−c)\mfp_c=(x-c)pc​=(x−c) for c∈Rc\in\RRc∈R, the points of the xxx-axis, with residue field A/pc=RA/\mfp_c=\RRA/pc​=R. Section 4 says more about how to read all this geometrically.

In both instances KKK has characteristic 000, so an irreducible fff is automatically separable. That is the one technical hypothesis needed for the facts quoted next.

The integral closure and the index

Let B~\BtB be the integral closure of AAA in LLL: the elements of LLL that satisfy a monic polynomial with coefficients in AAA. Then A⊆B⊆B~A\subseteq B\subseteq\BtA⊆B⊆B, since α\alphaα is integral and B~\BtB is a ring. We quote two facts; see Milne [6], Chapter 3.

  • B~\BtB is a Dedekind domain. In particular, every nonzero ideal of B~\BtB is invertible and factors uniquely into prime ideals.

    Remark

    We say a nonzero ideal III is invertible if there is another nonzero ideal JJJ such that IJIJIJ is principal.

  • B~\BtB is a finitely generated AAA-module. Since B~⊆L\Bt\subseteq LB⊆L and B⊆B~B\subseteq\BtB⊆B both span LLL over KKK, the quotient B~/B\Bt/BB/B is a finitely generated torsion AAA-module.

    Remark

    If RRR is an integral domain, and MMM is an RRR-module, then we say an element m∈Mm \in Mm∈M is torsion if there is some nonzero a∈Ra \in Ra∈R such that am=0am = 0am=0. We say MMM is a torsion module if every element of MMM is torsion.

For A=ZA=\ZZA=Z, the ring B~\BtB is the ring of integers OL\OO_LOL​. For A=R[x]A=\RR[x]A=R[x], the ring B~\BtB is the coordinate ring of the “desingularization” of CCC; Example 6 shows what this means in practice.

When AAA is a principal ideal domain, which covers both of our instances, the torsion module B~/B\Bt/BB/B is a direct sum ⨁jA/(dj)\bigoplus_j A/(d_j)⨁j​A/(dj​) by the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID (Dummit and Foote [7], Section 12.1), and we define the index to be [B~:B]=d1d2⋯dr∈A, [\Bt:B]=d_1d_2\cdots d_r\in A, [B:B]=d1​d2​⋯dr​∈A, well defined up to a unit. For A=ZA=\ZZA=Z this is the order of the finite group OL/Z[α]\OO_L/\ZZ[\alpha]OL​/Z[α], the usual index. For A=R[x]A=\RR[x]A=R[x] it is a polynomial whose roots are the points ccc over which BBB is “missing functions” that are in B~\BtB. The property of the index that matters is: p∤[B~:B]  ⟺  no nonzero element of B~/B is killed by p, \mfp\nmid[\Bt:B] \iff \text{no nonzero element of }\Bt/B\text{ is killed by }\mfp, p∤[B:B]⟺no nonzero element of B/B is killed by p, which is immediate from the decomposition into cyclic modules. We also recall the discriminant–index identity from the integral basis note, which holds over any PID with the same proof: disc⁡(f)=disc⁡(B)=[B~:B]2disc⁡(B~). \disc(f)=\disc(B)=[\Bt:B]^2\disc(\Bt). disc(f)=disc(B)=[B:B]2disc(B).

In a Dedekind domain every nonzero ideal is invertible.

Write p=(π)\mfp=(\pi)p=(π). Consider the ring homomorphism φ ⁣:B/πB→B~/πB~\varphi\colon B/\pi B\to\Bt/\pi\Btφ:B/πB→B/πB induced by B⊆B~B\subseteq\BtB⊆B.

It is worth stating this clearly, because the three parts are often run together.

4. Curve examples

Curves and their coordinate rings

Let f(x,y)∈R[x,y]f(x,y)\in\RR[x,y]f(x,y)∈R[x,y] be irreducible and monic in yyy, and let CCC be the curve f(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0 in the plane. A polynomial function on CCC is a polynomial h(x,y)h(x,y)h(x,y), regarded as a function on the points of CCC; two polynomials give the same function on CCC when their difference is a multiple of fff. So the ring of polynomial functions on CCC, its coordinate ring, is R[C]=R[x,y]/(f). \RR[C]=\RR[x,y]/(f). R[C]=R[x,y]/(f). This is the ring B=A[α]B=A[\alpha]B=A[α] of Section 1 with A=R[x]A=\RR[x]A=R[x] and α\alphaα the class of yyy. The subring A=R[x]A=\RR[x]A=R[x] consists of the functions on CCC that depend only on xxx, that is, the functions pulled back from the xxx-axis along the projection (x,y)↦x(x,y)\mapsto x(x,y)↦x.

Points of the curve CCC correspond to maximal ideals of R[C]\RR[C]R[C] with residue field R\RRR. A point P=(a,b)P=(a,b)P=(a,b) of CCC gives the ideal mP=(x−a, y−b)\mfm_P=(x-a,\,y-b)mP​=(x−a,y−b) of functions vanishing at PPP, and evaluation at PPP identifies R[C]/mP\RR[C]/\mfm_PR[C]/mP​ with R\RRR. The remaining maximal ideals of R[C]\RR[C]R[C] have residue field C\CCC, and each corresponds to a pair of complex conjugate points of CCC; we will meet these as “inert” primes.

Now fix c∈Rc\in\RRc∈R and the prime pc=(x−c)\mfp_c=(x-c)pc​=(x−c) of AAA. A maximal ideal of R[C]\RR[C]R[C] contains pc\mfp_cpc​ exactly when the corresponding point has xxx-coordinate ccc. So the primes of BBB over pc\mfp_cpc​ are the points of CCC on the vertical line x=cx=cx=c, real or complex, and B/pcB=R[x,y]/(f, x−c)=R[y]/(f(c,y)) B/\mfp_cB=\RR[x,y]/(f,\,x-c)=\RR[y]/(f(c,y)) B/pc​B=R[x,y]/(f,x−c)=R[y]/(f(c,y)) is the ring of functions on that fiber. Part I of Theorem 1 now reads: to find the points of CCC above ccc, substitute x=cx=cx=c into fff and factor the resulting polynomial in yyy. A linear factor y−by-by−b is a real point (c,b)(c,b)(c,b), an irreducible quadratic factor is a conjugate pair of complex points, and the exponent eie_iei​ is the multiplicity with which the vertical line meets CCC at that point.

Finally, the point PPP is nonsingular if the gradient (fx(P),fy(P))(f_x(P),f_y(P))(fx​(P),fy​(P)) is nonzero, and singular otherwise. This is where Lemma 2 meets geometry. The vector space mP/mP2\mfm_P/\mfm_P^2mP​/mP2​ is spanned by the classes of x−ax-ax−a and y−by-by−b, and Taylor expansion of fff at PPP gives the one relation fx(P) (x−a)+fy(P) (y−b)≡f(x,y)≡0 mod mP2. f_x(P)\,(x-a)+f_y(P)\,(y-b)\equiv f(x,y)\equiv 0\bmod{\mfm_P^2}. fx​(P)(x−a)+fy​(P)(y−b)≡f(x,y)≡0modmP2​. So dim⁡RmP/mP2\dim_\RR\mfm_P/\mfm_P^2dimR​mP​/mP2​ is 111 at a nonsingular point and 222 at a singular point, and by Lemma 2, the maximal ideal of a singular point is not invertible. Part II of Theorem 1 therefore applies to the fiber over ccc as soon as every point of CCC above ccc is nonsingular, and B=R[C]B=\RR[C]B=R[C] is a Dedekind domain exactly when CCC has no singular points at all. (For more on coordinate rings, see Fulton [8].)

Example 5 (The parabola y2=xy^2=xy2=x)

Let f=y2−xf=y^2-xf=y2−x, so CCC is the parabola y2=xy^2=xy2=x and B=R[x,y]/(y2−x)=R[y], B=\RR[x,y]/(y^2-x)=\RR[y], B=R[x,y]/(y2−x)=R[y], since x=y2x=y^2x=y2 on CCC. The vertical line x=0x=0x=0 is tangent to the parabola there, and the two points of the nearby fibers have come together: p0\mfp_0p0​ is ramified.
  • c<0c<0c<0. Then y2−cy^2-cy2−c is irreducible over R\RRR, so pcB\mfp_cBpc​B is prime with residue field R[y]/(y2−c)≅C\RR[y]/(y^2-c)\cong\CCR[y]/(y2−c)≅C, of degree 222. The parabola is a smooth curve, and BBB was already a Dedekind domain. The next example has a singular point, and it is the geometric picture of what goes wrong in Section 5.

The integral closure. The function t=y/xt=y/xt=y/x on CCC is the slope of the line from the origin, and on CCC it satisfies t2=y2x2=x+1, t^2=\frac{y^2}{x^2}=x+1, t2=x2y2​=x+1, so ttt is integral over A=R[x]A=\RR[x]A=R[x] but t∉Bt\notin Bt∈/B: ttt is a polynomial in xxx and yyy away from the origin, but not at the origin. B=R[t]. Geometrically B~\BtB is the coordinate ring of a line, and t↦(t2−1, t3−t)t\mapsto(t^2-1,\,t^3-t)t↦(t2−1,t3−t) maps the line onto CCC, passing through the origin twice, at t=1t=1t=1 and at t=−1t=-1t=−1, once along each branch. 5. Primes dividing the index

Return to A=ZA=\ZZA=Z, with α\alphaα an algebraic integer, K=Q(α)K=\QQ(\alpha)K=Q(α), B=Z[α]B=\ZZ[\alpha]B=Z[α], and B~=OK\Bt=\OO_KB=OK​. Here is the situation. The ring Z[α]\ZZ[\alpha]Z[α] is a Dedekind domain if and only if it is integrally closed, that is, if and only if [OK:Z[α]]=1[\OO_K:\ZZ[\alpha]]=1[OK​:Z[α]]=1. So whenever the index is bigger than 111, Part II of Theorem 1 is not available for Z[α]\ZZ[\alpha]Z[α] wholesale. But Part II only asks for the primes qi\mfq_iqi​ over the particular prime ppp to be invertible, and Part III says that when p∤[OK:Z[α]]p\nmid[\OO_K:\ZZ[\alpha]]p∤[OK​:Z[α]] the whole theorem transfers to OK\OO_KOK​. The following remark closes the circle: at a given ppp, the three conditions “Part II holds for Z[α]\ZZ[\alpha]Z[α],” “the qi\mfq_iqi​ are invertible,” and “p∤[OK:Z[α]]p\nmid[\OO_K:\ZZ[\alpha]]p∤[OK​:Z[α]]” are all the same.

Remark (Invertibility and the index are the same condition)

This remark uses localization and discrete valuation rings, which you may not have seen; read it for the shape of the argument. For a prime q\mfqq of BBB over ppp, the following are equivalent.

  1. q\mfqq is invertible.
  2. The local ring BqB_\mfqBq​ is a discrete valuation ring.
  3. Bq=B~qB_\mfq=\Bt_\mfqBq​=Bq​, that is, BBB and B~\BtB agree after inverting everything outside q\mfqq.

For (1)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(2): an invertible ideal is locally principal, and a Noetherian local domain of dimension 111 whose maximal ideal is principal is a DVR. For (2)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(3): a DVR is integrally closed, and B~q\Bt_\mfqBq​ is integral over BqB_\mfqBq​ inside the same fraction field. For (3)⇒\Rightarrow⇒(1): B~q\Bt_\mfqBq​ is a Dedekind domain, so qB~q\mfq\Bt_\mfqqBq​ is principal, and a finitely generated ideal that is locally principal is invertible.

Running over all primes qi\mfq_iqi​ above ppp, condition (3) for all of them says Bp=B~pB_p=\Bt_pBp​=Bp​ (inverting everything prime to ppp), which says that B~/B\Bt/BB/B has no ppp-torsion, which says p∤[B~:B]p\nmid[\Bt:B]p∤[B:B]. Together with the sharpness statement after Theorem 1: pZ[α]=∏iqiei  ⟺  every qi is invertible  ⟺  p∤[OK:Z[α]]. p\ZZ[\alpha]=\prod_i\mfq_i^{e_i} \iff \text{every }\mfq_i\text{ is invertible} \iff p\nmid[\OO_K:\ZZ[\alpha]]. pZ[α]=i∏​qiei​​⟺every qi​ is invertible⟺p∤[OK​:Z[α]]. For curves the same chain says: Part II holds over ccc if and only if no singular point lies above ccc, which is what we saw for the node.

So for a given prime ppp, Theorem 1 factors pOKp\OO_KpOK​ as soon as we can find some α∈OK\alpha\in\OO_Kα∈OK​ generating KKK whose index is prime to ppp, even if Z[α]≠OK\ZZ[\alpha]\neq\OO_KZ[α]=OK​. The next example shows the theorem being correct about Z[α]\ZZ[\alpha]Z[α] and silent about OK\OO_KOK​, and the one after it shows that sometimes no α\alphaα works.

6. Why primes dividing the discriminant ramify

Return to the general setting of Section 1, with AAA a PID. Recall that disc⁡(f)=∏i<j(αi−αj)2\disc(f)=\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2disc(f)=∏i<j​(αi​−αj​)2, where α1,…,αn\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_nα1​,…,αn​ are the roots of fff, and that this equals the discriminant disc⁡(B)\disc(B)disc(B) of the basis 1,α,…,αn−11,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}1,α,…,αn−1, the quantity computed with the trace matrix in the integral basis note. The discriminant is a universal polynomial with integer coefficients in the coefficients of fff, so it can be computed before or after reducing modulo p\mfpp: disc⁡(f‾)≡disc⁡(f)(modp). \disc(\overline{f})\equiv\disc(f)\pmod\mfp. disc(f​)≡disc(f)(modp). And a polynomial has a repeated root (in an algebraic closure) if and only if its discriminant vanishes. Putting this together with Kummer–Dedekind:

Theorem 9

Let p\mfpp be a prime of AAA with p∤[B~:B]\mfp\nmid[\Bt:B]p∤[B:B]; for instance any p\mfpp, if B=B~B=\BtB=B. Then p ramifies in B~  ⟺  p∣disc⁡(f)  ⟺  p∣disc⁡(B~). \mfp\text{ ramifies in }\Bt \iff \mfp\mid\disc(f) \iff \mfp\mid\disc(\Bt). p ramifies in B⟺p∣disc(f)⟺p∣disc(B).

Proof

By Part III, p\mfpp ramifies if and only if some ei≥2e_i\geq2ei​≥2, that is, if and only if f‾\overline{f}f​ has a repeated irreducible factor in k[x]k[x]k[x]. An irreducible polynomial over a perfect field (here kkk is finite or R\RRR) has distinct roots, so f‾\overline{f}f​ has a repeated irreducible factor if and only if it has a repeated root in an algebraic closure, if and only if disc⁡(f‾)=0\disc(\overline{f})=0disc(f​)=0, if and only if p∣disc⁡(f)\mfp\mid\disc(f)p∣disc(f). Remark (The general theorem, and why it is the same idea)

Dedekind's theorem on ramification says that for every number field and every prime ppp, with no hypothesis on indices, ppp ramifies in KKK if and only if p∣disc⁡(K)p\mid\disc(K)p∣disc(K). Theorem 9 proves this for all ppp not dividing the index of some Z[α]\ZZ[\alpha]Z[α], and for a common index divisor such as 222 in Example 8 it says nothing. (There, 2∤disc⁡(K)=−5032\nmid\disc(K)=-5032∤disc(K)=−503 and 222 is unramified, consistent with the general theorem.)

The general proof runs through the same mechanism, with the ring OK/pOK\OO_K/p\OO_KOK​/pOK​ in place of the polynomial f‾\overline{f}f​. Reducing an integral basis modulo ppp shows that disc⁡(K) mod p\disc(K)\bmod pdisc(K)modp is the discriminant of the trace form (x,y)↦Tr⁡(xy)(x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(xy)(x,y)↦Tr(xy) of the nnn-dimensional Fp\FpFp​-algebra R=OK/pOKR=\OO_K/p\OO_KR=OK​/pOK​, so p∣disc⁡(K)p\mid\disc(K)p∣disc(K) if and only if this trace form is degenerate. By the Chinese remainder theorem R≅∏iOK/qieiR\cong\prod_i\OO_K/\mfq_i^{e_i}R≅∏i​OK​/qiei​​, and the trace form of a product is the orthogonal sum of the trace forms of the factors. If some ei≥2e_i\geq2ei​≥2, the factor OK/qiei\OO_K/\mfq_i^{e_i}OK​/qiei​​ contains a nonzero nilpotent zzz, and then zyzyzy is nilpotent for every yyy, so Tr⁡(zy)=0\operatorname{Tr}(zy)=0Tr(zy)=0 for every yyy: the trace form is degenerate. If every ei=1e_i=1ei​=1, each factor is a finite field Fpfi\FF_{p^{f_i}}Fpfi​​, which is a separable extension of Fp\FpFp​, and the trace form of a separable extension is nondegenerate. So p∣disc⁡(K)  ⟺  R has nilpotents  ⟺  p ramifies. p\mid\disc(K)\iff R\text{ has nilpotents}\iff p\text{ ramifies.} p∣disc(K)⟺R has nilpotents⟺p ramifies. When R≅Fp[x]/(f‾)R\cong\Fp[x]/(\overline{f})R≅Fp​[x]/(f​), a nilpotent exists exactly when f‾\overline{f}f​ has a repeated factor, and that is Theorem 9. The Kummer–Dedekind theorem makes the nilpotents visible as repeated factors; the general theorem finds them without a polynomial to look at.
